lines.text: and that every future is the gift and blessing of God. Hence
the Christian does not allow his life to be determined by a
self-chosen aim, to which all his energies and hopes are bent;
but his life is rather characterized, in a certain sense, by lack
of specific aim, by which we mean an inner freedom from
self-chosen aims. The faith of the Christian is that the future
will bring him his true self, which he can never capture by
his own self-appointed courses. In other words, readiness for
my fate, for that which God designs to do with me.
Can we affirm that such readiness is ours? Are we prepared
to meet any destiny? Does our readiness to meet what the
future may bring give us freedom from our own obsessive
purposes? Are we, who aim at being Christians, characterized
by this note of inner freedom as Paul describes it:
"Let those who have wives live as though they had none,
and those who mourn as though they were not mourning,
and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and
those who buy as though they had no goods, and those
who deal with the world as though they had no dealings
with it."
Most men live, unconsciously to themselves, in a state of
characteristic inner discord. Their hopes for the future
without which they cannot live are combined with a fear
of the future which can rob them of what they already
possess. In so far as they strive to hold fast to what they
already possess, they are clinging desperately to the past and
not living towards the future but dying to it. What they hope
for from the future is always only something which, once
they have it, they will be eager to grasp and retain, so as to
possess it, and secure themselves against the future. It is
from such strivings of humanity, from such eagerness to hold
fast and possess, that there arises the curse which weighs on
the whole of human history; the strife of all against all,
because each wishes to assert himself and his rights and to
secure his future against others. And instead of living
accessibly to the future, men really live on the basis of the
past, which prescribes to them their aims, dictates their
motives and the criteria of their conduct. So, like nature,
